case_name: Sunder Singh v State of Uttaranchal
respondent:
State of Uttaranchal
Supreme Court of India

16 September 2010
Cr.A. No. 1164 of 2005
The Judgment was delivered by : V. S. Sirpurkar, J.
1. Appellant herein challenges the judgment of the High Court affirming the judgment passed by the Sessions Court. The Sessions Judge convicted the appellant/accused Sunder Singh for offences under Sections 302, 307 and 436, Indian Penal Code (IPC). While he was awarded the death sentence along with a fine of Rs.5,000/- and in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment for one year, he was given the punishment of seven years along with fine of Rs. 5,000/- and in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment for one year separately on the other two counts.
2. The incident in this case had taken place on 30.6.1989 in village Mahargheti, Patwari Circle Dangoli in the newly formed District Bageshwar (which was part of District Almora at the time of incident). In this ghastly incident, Pratap Singh, his wife Nandi Devi, his elder son
facts: The incident took place on 30.6.1989 in village Mahargheti, Patwari Circle Dangoli in the newly formed District Bageshwar (which was part of District Almora at the time of incident).
Five victims who lost their lives including Balwant Singh were roasted alive and died either on the spot or while being taken to the hospital or in the hospital.
The accused abjured his guilt. He raised the defence of false implication on account of the enmity due to land.
Shri Y.P. Singh who was appointed as Amicus Curiae urged before us that it could not be said that it was the accused who was the perpetrator of this crime.
issues: Whether the prosecution had proved that the accused had torched the ground floor room on the fateful day resulting in the victims being roasted alive.
Whether the accused had dealt a sword blow on Balwant Singh almost beheading him and on that count proceeded to convict the accused.
petitioner_arguments: The evidence of Vimla Devi (PW-1) could not be accepted as there were inherent pitfalls in her evidence. Firstly, she was an interested witness and secondly, her ability to see at night at 10 O'clock was suspect.
The so-called dying declaration by Prem Singh was also a suspect document and was not creditworthy.
This could not be said to be a rarest of rare case and the High Court has erred in affirming the death sentence.
respondent_arguments: The evidence of Vimla Devi (PW-1) was extremely important and credible and she was herself an injured witness.
There was nothing to suspect the dying declaration of Prem Singh.
This was a rarest of rare case.
court_reasoning: We have been taken through the whole evidence to show that there were contradictions and material omissions in her evidence.
The said dying declaration of Prem Singh did not have the endorsement of the doctor about Prem Singh being in fit condition to make a dying declaration.
It was further pointed out that there was nothing to suspect the dying declaration of Prem Singh.
holding: The High Court came to the conclusion that the Sessions Judge was right in convicting the accused. The High Court also endorsed the opinion of the Sessions Judge that this was a rarest of rare case and, therefore, affirmed the death sentence awarded to the accused by the Sessions Judge.
